title: Gangtok food guide: momos, phagshapa, gundruk and more
meta_description: What to eat in Gangtok: momos, thukpa, thenthuk, phagshapa, gundruk, sel roti, chhurpi and tongba. What each dish is, what it costs and where to find it.
summary: Gangtok eats from three kitchens: Nepali, Bhutia-Tibetan and Lepcha, with plains food alongside. Try momos and thenthuk, phagshapa (pork fat with radish and dried chilli), gundruk, sel roti and chhurpi cheese. A plate of momos costs ₹60–150 and a thali ₹150–300, indicative 2026. Eat in small places below MG Marg.

sections.heading: Three kitchens in one town
paras: Sikkim's food follows its people. The Nepali-speaking communities, today the majority, brought rice-dal-tarkari meals, fermented greens, sel roti and pickles. The Bhutia and Tibetan kitchen gave noodles, dumplings, butter tea and dishes of pork and beef. The Lepcha, the earliest people of Sikkim, have their own foods of forest greens, millet and fermented drinks, which you are most likely to taste in a village home. Add Marwari, Bengali and Punjabi plains food, and Gangtok's food is a fair map of who lives here.

Fermentation runs through all of it. Hill families had to store food through long monsoons and cold winters, so greens, soybeans, milk and millet were fermented, dried or smoked. That is why the most Sikkimese tastes are sour, smoky and sharp: gundruk, kinema, chhurpi and millet beer. Many of the vegetables are grown on Sikkim's certified organic farms, though rice and packaged food often come from the plains.

sections.heading: Dishes to try at least once
paras: Here is our shortlist for a first visit. Spellings vary from menu to menu, so ask by description if you cannot find the name.

Festivals bring their own food. Sel roti is fried in huge batches for Dashain and Tihar in October and November, and khapse fill Bhutia and Tibetan kitchens at Losar in February or March. If you are in Gangtok at those times, a host family or a homestay may well hand you a plate.
list: Momo: steamed or fried dumplings with pork, chicken, beef, vegetable or cheese filling, served with a fiery tomato-chilli sauce and a cup of soup.
Thukpa: noodle soup with vegetables or meat; the Gangtok version is often spicier than the Tibetan original.
Thenthuk: hand-pulled noodle soup, the dough torn straight into the pot. Best on a cold evening.
Phagshapa: strips of pork fat stewed with radish and dried red chillies, a Bhutia-Sikkimese classic. Rich and very spicy.
Gundruk: fermented and sun-dried leafy greens, served as a sour soup with rice or as a pickle.
Sel roti: a ring of sweet rice-flour batter, deep-fried. Eaten with tea or aloo dum, and at every festival.
Chhurpi: cheese made from buttermilk. Soft chhurpi goes into curries, soup and chutney; hard chhurpi is chewed slowly like a sweet that never ends.
Kinema: fermented soybean, a Limbu food, cooked as a pungent curry with rice. Strong smelling, very good.
Sha phaley: Tibetan bread stuffed with seasoned meat and cabbage, then fried. A filling snack.
Saag and ningro: mustard greens and fern shoots in season, stir-fried simply with garlic and chilli.
Khapse: crisp fried pastries made at Losar and other festivals.

sections.heading: Drinks: tongba, butter tea and Temi
paras: Tongba is millet beer served in a tall vessel, traditionally bamboo, packed with fermented millet. Hot water is poured over the grain and you sip through a bamboo straw, topping up with more hot water as you go. Chhang is the broader name for local grain beers. Both are mild but add up; drink slowly, especially if you are heading to Tsomgo or Nathu La the next morning, since alcohol and altitude do not mix.

Butter tea, or su cha, is salty tea churned with butter, more soup than tea to a plains palate. It is served in monasteries and Tibetan homes, and it does keep you warm. For ordinary tea, look for leaf from Temi, Sikkim's own tea estate in the south, sold in shops on and around MG Marg. Sweet milky tea is everywhere for ₹10–30 a cup, indicative 2026.

Sikkim also brews and distils, mainly in the south around Melli and Jorethang, and you will see local brands in every licensed shop. Drink in licensed places only; drinking in public on MG Marg is not allowed.

sections.heading: Where and how to eat
paras: MG Marg has the town's best-known cafes, bakeries and restaurants, and it is pleasant to eat with a view of the evening crowd. You pay a little more for that. For everyday food at local prices, walk down the lanes below MG Marg towards Lal Bazaar, or along Tibet Road and Paljor Stadium Road, where small momo and thali places feed office workers and students. A busy place with a quick turnover is usually the freshest.

Lal Bazaar is worth a visit for food even if you do not cook. The market, housed in the Kanchendzonga Shopping Complex, has a vegetable floor, and on Sunday mornings village sellers come in for the haat with greens, chhurpi, dried fish and festive breads. Look for sidra, dried fish, and sukuti, dried meat, often cooked with chillies into a sharp side dish.

In December, the Gangtok Food and Culture Festival is held on MG Marg, with stalls from across the state. It is the easiest way to taste many local dishes in one evening. Dates change each year, so check current status before you travel.

For the most home-style Sikkimese food, stay a night or two in a village homestay at Aritar, Rhenock, Rumtek or Ranka, or, for Indian citizens with a permit, Zuluk. Meals are cooked from the family's garden and the pickles are usually homemade.

Gangtok eats early. Breakfast places open around 7 am, lunch is from about noon, and many small eateries close by 8–9 pm, with restaurants on MG Marg staying open a little later. If you arrive on a late jeep from Siliguri, ask your hotel to keep dinner for you, or eat on the way at one of the roadside halts on NH10.

sections.heading: Vegetarian, Jain and other diets
paras: Vegetarians eat well in Gangtok. Every momo shop has vegetable and cheese momos, and thalis, dal, saag, gundruk soup, aloo dum and chhurpi dishes are all vegetarian. Many hotels and restaurants serving visitors from the plains run separate vegetarian kitchens; ask if that matters to you.

Jain food without onion, garlic or root vegetables is harder, but several hotels and restaurants used to Gujarati and Marwari guests can cook it with a day's notice. Tell your hotel when you book. Gluten-free travellers should know that momos, thukpa, thenthuk and sha phaley are all wheat-based; rice, dal and vegetable dishes are the safer choice.

Pork and beef are both common in Gangtok, especially in Bhutia, Tibetan and Nepali dishes. If you avoid either, ask before you order momos or soups, since the filling is not always written on the menu.

sections.heading: Eating safely and politely
paras: Gangtok's food is generally safe, and a few habits keep it that way.
list: Drink filtered or boiled water and carry a refillable bottle; most hotels will fill it.
Start gently with chilli. Sikkim's round dalle chillies are among the hottest you will meet; ask for the sauce on the side.
Chew hard chhurpi slowly and carefully, and skip it if you have dental work.
Eat light before a Tsomgo or Nathu La day; a heavy, greasy breakfast and altitude are a bad pair.
In homes and monasteries, accept tea with both hands and take at least a sip; you can leave the rest.
Do not waste food at a homestay. Take a small first helping and ask for more.
Carry your own cloth bag for market shopping; plastic is discouraged across Sikkim.

faqs.q: What is the famous food of Gangtok
faqs.a: Momos are the best known, followed by thukpa and thenthuk noodle soups. For truly Sikkimese tastes, try phagshapa (pork fat stewed with radish and dried chillies), gundruk (fermented greens), sel roti (a ring-shaped rice bread), chhurpi cheese and kinema (fermented soybean). Tongba, a millet beer sipped through a bamboo straw, is the classic local drink.

Phagshapa is a Bhutia-Sikkimese dish of pork fat, often with some meat, stewed with radish and dried red chillies. It is rich, oily and very spicy, and is usually eaten with steamed rice. You will find it in local restaurants and homestays rather than tourist cafes. Expect to pay around ₹150–500 with rice, indicative 2026, depending on the place.

faqs.q: Where can I eat cheap momos in Gangtok
faqs.a: In the small eateries on the lanes below MG Marg towards Lal Bazaar, and along Tibet Road and Paljor Stadium Road. A plate costs ₹60–100 in these places, against ₹120–250 in MG Marg restaurants, indicative 2026. Choose a busy shop with a quick turnover for the freshest momos, and ask about the filling if you avoid pork or beef.

Yes. Vegetable and cheese momos, thalis, dal, saag, gundruk soup, aloo dum and chhurpi dishes are vegetarian and easy to find. Many hotels serving visitors from the plains keep separate vegetarian kitchens. Jain food without onion, garlic or root vegetables is harder but possible with notice; tell your hotel when you book.

faqs.q: What is chhurpi and how do I eat it
faqs.a: Chhurpi is a cheese made from buttermilk. Soft chhurpi, like fresh ricotta, is cooked with greens, made into soup or ground into a chilli chutney. Hard chhurpi is pressed, dried and smoked into small blocks that you hold in your mouth and chew slowly as they soften. It is very hard, so take care if you have dental work.

Tongba is a millet beer served in a tall vessel, traditionally bamboo, packed with fermented millet. Hot water is poured over the grain, and you sip through a bamboo straw, topping up with more water. It tastes mild and slightly sour, and costs about ₹150–400, indicative 2026. Drink it slowly, and not the night before a high-altitude trip.

faqs.q: When is the Gangtok food festival
faqs.a: The Gangtok Food and Culture Festival is held on MG Marg in December, with stalls from across Sikkim selling local dishes, drinks and crafts. It is the easiest way to taste many Sikkimese foods in one evening. Exact dates change from year to year, so check current status before you travel and book hotels early for that week.

faqs.q: Can I buy local food products to take home from Gangtok
faqs.a: Yes. Large cardamom, ginger, turmeric, buckwheat flour, dried chillies and Temi tea all travel well and are sold in shops around MG Marg and at Lal Bazaar. Hard chhurpi also keeps for weeks. Homemade pickles are good but pack them in a sealed jar inside a bag, because airline and bus luggage gets thrown around.

faqs.q: Is street food in Gangtok safe
faqs.a: Generally yes, if you use common sense. Eat at busy stalls and small eateries where food is cooked fresh in front of you, avoid cut fruit that has been standing, and drink filtered or boiled water. Momos and soups are served hot, which helps. Go easy on chilli sauce for the first day or two while your stomach adjusts.
